title: Supervised Learning Methods
description: Models, objectives, and evaluation for labeled prediction tasks.

questions.prompt: In supervised learning, what is the target variable?
options: The quantity or class the model is trained to predict
The order in which rows are stored
questions.explanation: The target supplies the desired output for each labeled training example.

questions.prompt: What does ordinary linear regression predict?
options: A weighted sum of input features
questions.explanation: Linear regression models a continuous response as a linear combination of features, often with an intercept.

questions.prompt: Which statements about logistic regression are generally correct?
options: It can model binary class probabilities
It uses a logistic link for its linear score
It is inherently a deep neural network
A decision threshold converts scores to classes
questions.explanation: Logistic regression maps a linear score to probabilities; thresholding can produce class labels.

questions.prompt: Feature scaling can matter for distance-based k-nearest-neighbor models.
questions.explanation: Features with larger numeric ranges can dominate distance calculations unless scales are considered.

questions.prompt: A decision-tree classifier typically chooses a split to do what?
options: Improve class purity or reduce an impurity measure
Minimize the number of labels in the dataset
questions.explanation: Tree splits are selected to reduce impurity, such as Gini impurity or entropy, in child nodes.

questions.prompt: What does a support vector machine seek to maximize in its basic classification form?
questions.explanation: A maximum-margin classifier seeks a separating boundary with the largest margin, with regularization for violations.

questions.prompt: Which metrics require predicted class labels at a chosen threshold?
options: ROC AUC in its usual score-based form
questions.explanation: Precision, recall, and F1 use thresholded predictions. ROC AUC normally uses ranking scores across thresholds.

questions.prompt: What does specificity measure?
options: The fraction of actual negatives predicted negative
The fraction of predicted positives that are correct
The fraction of all predictions correct
questions.explanation: Specificity is true-negative rate: TN/(TN+FP).

questions.prompt: An R-squared value of 0.9 means the model is correct on exactly 90% of examples.
questions.explanation: R-squared is a variance-based goodness-of-fit statistic, not a classification accuracy percentage.

questions.prompt: If a regression target is measured in seconds, what units does mean absolute error have?
questions.explanation: Absolute errors retain the target units, making MAE directly interpretable in the original scale.

questions.prompt: What are common properties of one-hot encoding a nominal category?
options: It avoids imposing a numeric order on categories
It may create many columns for high-cardinality features
It always preserves a compact representation
questions.explanation: One-hot indicators avoid ordinal assumptions but can be wide when a feature has many distinct categories.

questions.prompt: When is ordinal encoding most defensible?
questions.explanation: Ordinal codes are meaningful when category order is real; otherwise the values may imply a false ordering.

questions.prompt: A stratified classification split aims to preserve class proportions across partitions.
questions.explanation: Stratification helps each split represent the overall class distribution, especially with imbalanced labels.

questions.prompt: What does macro-averaged recall do across classes?
options: Compute recall per class, then give each class equal weight
Pool all examples before computing one recall
Weight classes by their training frequency only
questions.explanation: Macro averaging gives each class equal contribution regardless of how many examples it contains.

questions.prompt: Why can strong multicollinearity be problematic for interpreting linear-model coefficients?
options: Individual coefficient estimates can become unstable
It necessarily lowers predictive performance to zero
questions.explanation: Correlated predictors make it harder to attribute effects uniquely, increasing coefficient uncertainty.

questions.prompt: Which are reasonable options for handling missing feature values?
options: Add a missingness indicator when informative
Use a model that supports missing values
Replace all missing values with the target label
questions.explanation: Imputation, indicators, or capable models are possible; target values must never be copied into features.

questions.prompt: What can a learning curve help diagnose?
options: How training and validation performance change with data or training size
questions.explanation: Learning curves reveal patterns such as high bias, high variance, and whether more data may help.

questions.prompt: All trees in a random forest are trained on exactly the same examples and feature set.
questions.explanation: Random forests introduce randomness through bootstrap samples and feature subsampling to diversify trees.

questions.prompt: What does log loss penalize especially strongly?
options: Assigning very low probability to the true class
questions.explanation: Log loss becomes large when the model gives the observed class a probability near zero.

questions.prompt: What should guide selection of a classifier decision threshold?
options: The relative costs of false positives and false negatives
questions.explanation: Choose thresholds using validation evidence and the application’s error costs; repeated test-set tuning contaminates final evaluation.
